nodes.name: Formalization Approach
nodes.statement: Implementation note: Instead of formalizing the full abstract theory of frame presentations (which would require constructing free frames and frame congruences), we use a concrete approach for the Zariski locale. For the frame Rad(R) of radical ideals, we prove: item Generation: Every radical ideal is the supremum of basic opens: I = bigvee_f in I D(f) This is Rad.radical\_eq\_sSup\_basicOpen. item Universal property: A frame homomorphism from Rad(R) is uniquely determined by its action on basic opens: (forall f in R,\, varphi(D(f)) = psi(D(f))) implies varphi = psi This is Rad.frameHom\_eq\_of\_basicOpen\_eq. \label{remark:concrete-approach}
  \textbf{Implementation note:} Instead of formalizing the full abstract theory of frame presentations
  (which would require constructing free frames and frame congruences), we use a concrete approach
  for the Zariski locale.

  For the frame $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ of radical ideals, we prove:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Generation:} Every radical ideal is the supremum of basic opens:
          $$I = \bigvee_{f \in I} D(f)$$
          This is \texttt{Rad.radical\_eq\_sSup\_basicOpen}.

    \item \textbf{Universal property:} A frame homomorphism from $\mathrm{Rad}(R)$ is uniquely
          determined by its action on basic opens:
          $$(\forall f \in R,\, \varphi(D(f)) = \psi(D(f))) \implies \varphi = \psi$$
          This is \texttt{Rad.frameHom\_eq\_of\_basicOpen\_eq}.
  \end{enumerate}

  These concrete theorems provide the same practical power as the abstract presentation
  $\mathrm{Fr}\langle D(f) : f \in R \mid \text{relations} \rangle$ without requiring the
  full infrastructure of quotients of free frames.

  \begin{enumerate}

Recall that for radical ideals:
  \begin{align*}
    I \land K_j &:= I \cap K_j \\
    \bigvee_j K_j &:= \sqrt{\sum_j K_j} \\
    I \land \bigvee_j K_j &:= I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j}
  \end{align*}
  
  We need to show:
  $$I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j} = \sqrt{\sum_j (I \cap K_j)}$$
  
  \textbf{Right side is radical:} Since $I \cap K_j$ is radical for each $j$ (intersection of radicals), 
  and the radical of a sum of radical ideals is radical, the right side is radical.
  
  \textbf{Inclusion $\subseteq$:} Let $x \in I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j}$.
  
  Then $x \in I$ and $x^n \in \sum_j K_j$ for some $n$.
  
  Write $x^n = \sum_j y_j$ with $y_j \in K_j$.
  
  Then:
  \begin{align*}
    x^{2n} &= (x^n)^2 = (\sum_j y_j)^2 = \sum_j y_j^2 + \sum_{j \neq k} y_j y_k
  \end{align*}
  
  Each $y_j^2 \in K_j$ (as $K_j$ is an ideal). For cross terms, since $x \in I$ we have $x \cdot y_j y_k \in I$ as well.
  
  More carefully: we have $x^n = \sum_j y_j$, so $x \cdot x^n = x^{n+1} = x \sum_j y_j = \sum_j x y_j$.
  
  Since $x \in I$, each term $xy_j \in I$. Also $y_j \in K_j$, so $xy_j \in I \cap K_j$.
  
  Therefore $x^{n+1} = \sum_j xy_j \in \sum_j (I \cap K_j)$, giving $x \in \sqrt{\sum_j(I \cap K_j)}$.
  
  \textbf{Inclusion $\supseteq$:} Let $x \in \sqrt{\sum_j (I \cap K_j)}$.
  
  Then $x^m \in \sum_j (I \cap K_j)$ for some $m$, so $x^m = \sum_j z_j$ with $z_j \in I \cap K_j$.
  
  Then:
  \begin{align*}
    x^m &= \sum_j z_j \in \sum_j K_j \quad \text{(since } z_j \in K_j \text{)} \\
    x &\in \sqrt{\sum_j K_j}
  \end{align*}
  
  Also, $z_j \in I$ for all $j$ means $x^m = \sum_j z_j \in I$ (as $I$ is an ideal).
  
  Since $I$ is radical and $x^m \in I$, we have $x \in I$.
  
  Therefore $x \in I \cap \sqrt{\sum_j K_j}$.

nodes.name: Frame-Primeness vs Ring-Primeness
nodes.statement: Frame-theoretic primeness and ring-theoretic primeness are dual notions, not equivalent. Frame-primeness (join-prime from below: I leq J vee K Rightarrow I leq J or I leq K) differs from ring-primeness (meet-prime from above: JK subseteq I Rightarrow J subseteq I or K subseteq I). Counterexample: In Z/6Z, the zero ideal (0) is frame-prime but not ring-prime (2 cdot 3 = 0 in (0) but 2, 3 notin (0)).
conclusions: Frame-theoretic primeness and ring-theoretic primeness are dual notions, not equivalent.

\label{thm:prime-ideals-specialization}
  
  
  
  Frame-theoretic primeness and ring-theoretic primeness are \textbf{dual} notions, not equivalent.
  Frame-primeness (join-prime from below: $I \leq J \vee K \Rightarrow I \leq J$ or $I \leq K$) differs from
  ring-primeness (meet-prime from above: $JK \subseteq I \Rightarrow J \subseteq I$ or $K \subseteq I$).

  Counterexample: In $\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}$, the zero ideal $(0)$ is frame-prime but not ring-prime
  ($2 \cdot 3 = 0 \in (0)$ but $2, 3 \notin (0)$).
